opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest lesson is that Jensen is extremely clear about what matters most, and he's willing to say no to a lot of things in order to go all-in on that.

At NVIDIA, there are always many good ideas. Researchers are smart people, and every project can look promising. But Jensen often asks a very simple question: is this something only we can do, and is it important enough to change the world? If the answer isn't clearly yes, then maybe it's not where we should put our best people and our compute. That forces you to think about priority in terms of impact, not just interest.

Another thing I've learned is that his priorities are set on a very long time horizon. When we started working on things like world foundation models and physical AI, it wasn't obvious to everyone that this would pay off soon. But he looks at where computing is going five or ten years from now and works backward. Once he decides something is important, the commitment is very strong. It's not "let's try a little bit and see." It's "this is going to matter, so let's build the full stack for it."

He also has a way of keeping the organization flat and close to the information. He talks directly to people working on the problem, so prioritization isn't filtered through many layers. That means decisions can be made quickly, and if the priority needs to change, it changes quickly too. That speed is itself a kind of advantage.

For me personally, as someone leading a research team, it changed how I think about my own job. It's not about doing as many interesting projects as possible. It's about identifying the one or two things that, if we get them right, will really move the field, and then protecting the team's focus so they can actually get there. Saying no is hard, especially to good ideas, but I've come to see it as one of the most important things a leader does.

fable-5.1.text:
One thing I've really taken from Jensen is that prioritization isn't about making a long list and ranking it. It's about being very clear on the one or two things that actually matter, and then being willing to say no to almost everything else, even things that look attractive.

When I first joined NVIDIA, I came from a research mindset where you explore many directions in parallel, because you don't know which one will work. Jensen thinks differently. He asks: what is the thing that, if we don't do it, nothing else matters? And then he puts a disproportionate amount of the company's energy there. With CUDA, with deep learning, and now with generative AI and physical AI, he saw the direction early and committed before it was obvious to everyone else. That commitment is the prioritization.

The second thing is that he prioritizes based on where the world is going, not where it is today. He often says you should build for the future that you believe in, not for the market that exists right now. That changes how you allocate resources. You don't optimize for this quarter's revenue, you optimize so that when the inflection happens, you're already there.

And the third thing, which I think is underappreciated, is how he uses urgency. He talks about the company being thirty days from going out of business. It's not literally true, but it creates a mindset where you can't afford to spread yourself thin. You have to pick, and you have to move fast on what you picked.

For my own team, working on world models and generative AI for physical systems, this has really shaped how I lead. There are endless interesting research problems. But I try to ask the same question: what is the capability that, if we get it right, unlocks everything downstream? And then we focus there, and we accept that some interesting side projects simply won't get done. That's hard for researchers, but I've come to believe it's the right way to build something that matters.

astra-6.text:
The lesson I take from Jensen’s approach is that prioritization means deciding what you’re willing not to do. You can have many good ideas, but if you spread your attention across all of them, you may never give the most important one enough attention to succeed.

In research, that means looking beyond whether a problem is interesting and asking: If we solve it, what does it unlock? That question helps distinguish work that is intellectually appealing from work that could really change what’s possible. And as you learn more, you have to be willing to revisit those priorities.

sol-6.1.text: What I take from Jensen’s approach is that prioritization means deciding what deserves your attention—and being willing to let other things wait. In research, there are always more interesting ideas than you can pursue. The hard part is asking, “Which problem matters most, and where can I make a meaningful contribution?” Then you have to give that problem enough focus to make real progress. Being busy is easy; choosing well is much harder.
